title: Design a WhatsApp-style chat
scopeHtml: Scope: requirements, API, estimates, connection gateways, routing and ordering, groups, presence, offline and push, E2EE. Questions are still to be written.

notes.title: Requirements
notes.html:
WhatsApp-style chat lets two people (or a group) exchange messages instantly, shows delivery state (sent, delivered, read), works with flaky phones that go offline, and keeps messages private. Others: Telegram, Signal, iMessage, Messenger. The tricky parts are millions of long-lived connections, never losing or duplicating a message, per-chat ordering, and offline delivery.

Functional requirements

  • 1:1 and group chat (up to 1,024 members for WhatsApp-like groups), text plus media.
  • Delivery receipts: sent (server has it), delivered (device has it), read.
  • Online/last seen, typing indicator.
  • Offline delivery: a message is stored until the recipient comes online; push notification when offline.
  • Multi-device sync; message history on a new device (optional).
  • End-to-end encryption (E2EE) as a design constraint.

Non-functional requirements

  • Delivery latency under 200 ms when both are online.
  • Zero message loss once the server acknowledges; no duplicates visible to the user.
  • Per-conversation ordering.
  • Hundreds of millions of concurrent connections; high availability.

Decision gravity. Choose a persistent bidirectional connection (WebSocket or custom protocol over TCP) with application-level acknowledgements. Long polling or HTTP per message would multiply latency and battery use. One-way door: the protocol (ack scheme, message ids) is baked into every client you ship, and old app versions live for years.

Everyday analogy. A post office with a permanent pneumatic tube to every house; if nobody is home, letters wait in a box until the door opens.

Common interview traps.

  • Forgetting offline users and push notifications.
  • Not stating the delivery guarantee (at-least-once plus dedupe).
  • Skipping group chats and multi-device, which change fan-out design.

notes.title: API
notes.html:
Mostly a streaming protocol, plus REST for the non-realtime bits.

// Client to server over the persistent connection (JSON shown for readability;
// production protocols use compact binary such as Protobuf)
{ "type":"send", "clientMsgId":"c-7f31", "chatId":"chat_551", "to":"u_9",
  "ciphertext":"<base64>", "ts":1731150000123 }

// Server ack to sender (message persisted)
{ "type":"ack", "clientMsgId":"c-7f31", "serverMsgId":"m_90017", "state":"SENT", "seq":412 }

// Server pushes to recipient
{ "type":"msg", "serverMsgId":"m_90017", "chatId":"chat_551", "from":"u_3", "seq":412, "ciphertext":"..." }

// Recipient device acks
{ "type":"delivered", "serverMsgId":"m_90017" }
{ "type":"read", "chatId":"chat_551", "uptoSeq":412 }
POST /v1/media/upload-url       -> { "uploadUrl":"https://.../presigned", "mediaId":"md_5" }
GET  /v1/chats/chat_551/messages?afterSeq=400&limit=100      // catch-up after reconnect
POST /v1/groups  { "name":"Family", "members":["u_1","u_2"] } -> 201 { "groupId":"g_8" }
GET  /v1/users/u_9/keys         -> pre-key bundle for E2EE session setup

clientMsgId is the idempotency key: a retried send maps to the same message. seq is a per-chat monotonically increasing number that gives order and makes gaps detectable. Media bytes bypass the chat servers (presigned upload; the message carries the media id and decryption key).

Industry example. WhatsApp used a modified XMPP, later a custom binary protocol over a persistent TCP connection on Erlang servers; Signal uses a WebSocket to its server for the same job.

Everyday analogy. Registered post with a tracking number: you can re-send safely and the receiver can tell if one in the sequence is missing.

Common interview traps.

  • No client-generated id (retries create duplicates).
  • Ordering by timestamp only (clocks differ).
  • Sending media through the chat connection.

notes.title: Estimates
notes.html:
Assume 500M DAU, 100M concurrent connections at peak, 40 messages sent per user per day.

Quantity Calculation Result
Messages 500M x 40 20B/day, 230k/s avg, peak 700k/s
Deliveries groups multiply; assume 1.5 recipients avg ~350k to 1M deliveries/s
Message size ~100 B text + ~100 B metadata (E2EE ciphertext adds overhead) ~200 B
Storage (if retained) 20B x 200 B 4 TB/day, ~1.5 PB/year
Connections 100M concurrent / ~500k per big server 200 servers minimum; plan ~400 for headroom
Connection memory 100M x ~10 KB state ~1 TB across the fleet
Presence updates each connect/disconnect tens of thousands/s, handled lazily
Media 10% of messages x 200 KB 400 TB/day at CDN/object storage

What this tells you. The scarce resource is concurrent connections, not request rate. WhatsApp famously ran about 1-2 million connections per Erlang server in 2012 (about 2M on a tuned box, per their public posts). Messages are small. Media dominates bytes. A key design choice: WhatsApp-style systems keep messages only until delivered (server as a mailbox), cutting storage by two orders of magnitude compared with retaining history forever.

Everyday analogy. A switchboard with 100 million phone lines but short calls.

Common interview traps.

  • Sizing by requests per second and ignoring connection counts, file descriptors, and memory per connection.
  • Storing all history on servers when the product keeps it on devices.
  • Forgetting group fan-out amplification.

notes.title: High-level design
notes.html:
Components

  • Gateway (connection) servers: hold the WebSocket/TCP connections, do TLS, heartbeat, framing; stateless apart from the live socket. Each connection is identified by (userId, deviceId).
  • Session registry: a fast map userId -> [gatewayId, deviceId, lastSeen] in Redis (or an in-house service). Updated on connect/disconnect with TTL refreshed by heartbeats.
  • Chat service: validates, assigns the per-chat seq, persists, acks the sender, routes to recipients.
  • Message store: durable per-recipient mailbox/inbox: Cassandra/ScyllaDB or HBase (WhatsApp used Mnesia/Erlang early, Facebook Messenger used HBase, Discord moved from Cassandra to ScyllaDB). Partition by chatId (or recipient inbox), cluster by seq.
  • Push notifier: sends wake-ups via APNs (Apple) and FCM (Android) when the recipient is offline.
  • Media service: presigned upload to object storage, CDN download; thumbnails.
  • Group service: membership, roles, group key management.

Online path steps

  1. A sends over its socket to Gateway 1.
  2. Chat service persists the message with seq and acks A (one grey tick).
  3. Router looks up B in the session registry, pushes via B's gateway.
  4. B's device acks delivery (two ticks); server forwards the state to A. When B opens the chat, a read receipt follows (blue ticks).

Offline path: no session entry, so the message stays in B's mailbox, a push notification is sent; when B reconnects it fetches everything after its last seq and acks.

Decision gravity. Persist before ack. The sender's single tick means "the server owns this message". That is the durability commitment; the cost is a write on the critical path (about 5 ms to a Cassandra quorum), reversible only by weakening the guarantee, which users would feel as lost messages.

Industry examples. WhatsApp: Erlang/FreeBSD, mailbox model, messages deleted from servers after delivery; Discord: Elixir gateways, Cassandra to ScyllaDB for history; Slack: WebSocket gateways plus MySQL (Vitess).

Everyday analogy. The server is the mailbox at the building entrance; delivery to the flat happens when the person is home.

Common interview traps.

  • Direct server-to-server delivery without a durable store in the middle.
  • Acking the sender before persisting.
  • One global session registry as a single point of failure.

notes.title: Deep dives
notes.html:
Connections and the gateway layer

A modern Linux server can hold 1M+ idle TCP connections if tuned: raise file descriptors (ulimit -n 2000000, fs.file-max), widen ephemeral ports on the load balancer side, use epoll/kqueue with an event loop (Netty, Erlang BEAM, Go, Elixir), and keep per-connection memory small (4 to 10 KB).

# Kernel and limits sketch for a gateway host
sysctl -w fs.file-max=3000000
sysctl -w net.core.somaxconn=65535
sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_tw_reuse=1
ulimit -n 2000000
  • Heartbeats: application ping every 30 to 60 s (mobile NATs drop idle TCP after minutes); missing 2 pings marks the connection dead and removes the registry entry. Mobile uses adaptive intervals to save battery.
  • Load balancing: L4 balancer (least connections) in front; connections are long-lived so round robin makes uneven servers; draining on deploy with gradual reconnect.
  • Reconnect storms: a deploy of 200 gateways kicks 100M clients which reconnect at once. Mitigate with client jittered exponential backoff (random 1 to 30 s), rolling deploys (a few % at a time), connection draining over minutes, and admission control at the gateway.

Decision gravity. Keep gateways thin and nearly stateless: they only terminate sockets and forward frames. This makes deploys and crashes survivable (clients reconnect and catch up from seq). Alternative: put chat logic in the gateway (fewer hops, harder to deploy). Reversible with effort.

Production incident pattern. Symptom: after a deploy, message delay of minutes and a 10x spike in CPU. Metric: new connections per second, auth service latency. Cause: reconnect storm saturating login and registry. Fix: backoff with jitter, rate-limited accepts, deploy canaries.

Everyday analogy. A hotel lobby with a front desk that connects calls but does not remember conversations.

Common interview traps.

  • Forgetting that mobile networks silently kill idle connections.
  • Using HTTP long polling for a billion users.
  • Deploying all gateways at once.

Routing, ordering and delivery guarantees

Routing: to find B's gateway, look up the session registry. If B is on another data centre or has several devices, route to all device sessions. Large systems shard users to "home" chat servers by consistent hashing so the chat service for B (which also owns B's inbox) is determined by hash(userId); the sender's gateway forwards to B's owning node directly.

Ordering: wall-clock timestamps are not reliable. Assign a per-chat sequence number at the chat service: a counter owned by the partition that owns the chat (single writer per chat) gives strict order. For 1:1 chats the inbox of the recipient can be ordered by arrival at the server. Clients display by seq, then local time for unsent ones.

Delivery guarantee: at-least-once + dedupe = effectively once.

  • Sender retries send with the same clientMsgId until it gets the ack.
  • Server dedupes by (chatId, clientMsgId) (a unique key in the store, or a short-lived Redis set) and returns the original serverMsgId.
  • Recipient acks delivered; the server deletes (or marks) the message in its mailbox only after the ack; unacked messages are redelivered on reconnect, and the client dedupes by serverMsgId.
-- Cassandra-style model (CQL)
CREATE TABLE messages (
  chat_id   text,
  seq       bigint,
  server_msg_id text,
  sender    text,
  ciphertext blob,
  sent_at   timestamp,
  PRIMARY KEY ((chat_id), seq)
) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (seq DESC);
-- Idempotency via lightweight transaction or a separate dedupe table keyed by (chat_id, client_msg_id)

Gap detection: if a client receives seq 415 after 412, it asks GET messages?afterSeq=412 to fill 413 and 414.

Decision gravity. Sequence per chat from a single writer is the choice that gives order cheaply; alternatives (Lamport/vector clocks, global sequence) cost more or serialise too much. It breaks if one chat becomes a hotspot (a huge public group) so large groups use sharded streams. Changing the ordering scheme later is a one-way door visible to users as reordered history.

Everyday analogy. Numbering each page of a letter so the reader can spot a missing page and ask for it again.

Common interview traps.

  • Claiming exactly-once delivery over the network.
  • Using client timestamps for ordering.
  • Deleting from the mailbox before the recipient's ack.

Groups and fan-out

For a group of N members, one send becomes N deliveries. Two strategies:

  • Fan-out on write (per-member inbox): copy a reference of the message to each member's inbox. Fast reads, write amplification N (for N=1,024 that is 1,024 writes per message).
  • Group stream (fan-out on read): store the message once in the group's stream; each member keeps a cursor (lastReadSeq). Writes are 1, reads are N (but each member reads only when active). Works well for big groups and channels (Telegram channels, Discord, Slack).

WhatsApp-sized groups (up to 1,024) use fan-out on write with small payloads; big communities use the stream model. Group E2EE uses sender keys: each member distributes a sender key to others once, and each message is encrypted once with the sender's key, so the server stores one ciphertext rather than N.

Membership changes (removing someone) need key rotation so they cannot read future messages.

Decision gravity. Group size limits are product decisions that quietly protect the architecture (a 1,024 cap keeps fan-out bounded). Raising limits later forces the stream model, a heavy migration.

Industry example. WhatsApp group limit moved from 256 to 512 to 1,024 members; Discord and Telegram use stream/channel models with millions of members.

Everyday analogy. A noticeboard in the club (stream) versus a photocopy placed in every member's pigeonhole (inbox).

Common interview traps.

  • Treating a 100k-member group as 100k inbox writes per message.
  • Forgetting key rotation on member removal.

Presence, typing and receipts

Presence (online, last seen) is high-churn data; do not persist every change. Keep lastSeen in the registry (updated with heartbeats, flushed to a DB every few minutes). A user's contacts subscribe to their presence only when the chat is open; broadcasting presence to 500 contacts for every flap would multiply load. Debounce flaps (do not announce offline for 10 s after disconnect) and send typing events through the existing connection with a 3 s expiry and no persistence.

Read receipts are batched: send read upto seq, not one per message. Privacy setting to hide last seen/read receipts is checked on the server before sending.

Common interview traps.

  • Persisting each typing event.
  • Fan-out of presence to all contacts.
  • Per-message read receipts instead of a cursor.

Offline delivery, push and multi-device

When B is offline: message waits in B's mailbox (TTL 30 days in WhatsApp-like systems, then dropped). The push notifier sends a generic wake-up through APNs/FCM (with E2EE the push often carries no content, only "you have a message", so the phone wakes the app which fetches and decrypts). Push is unreliable (throttled, collapsed), so it is a hint; the source of truth is the mailbox fetched on connect.

Multi-device: each device has its own identity key, session and mailbox cursor. The sender encrypts per recipient device (Signal protocol fan-out), or a linked device syncs history from the primary (WhatsApp's earlier model) / server-assisted encrypted backup (newer). Server routes to all active devices; receipts from any device count as delivered.

Decision gravity. Treating push as a hint and the mailbox as truth means you can lose pushes without losing messages. The per-device encryption sessions are a significant complexity cost to accept for E2EE; it is a one-way door for the product's privacy promise.

Everyday analogy. The doorbell tells you there is a parcel; the parcel is in the locker whether you hear the bell or not.

Common interview traps.

  • Relying on push notifications to carry the message.
  • Single-device mental model for multi-device.
  • Putting message text in push payloads for an E2EE product.

End-to-end encryption in one page

The server must not read messages. Signal protocol (used by WhatsApp, Signal, Messenger secret chats): each user publishes a pre-key bundle (identity key, signed pre-key, one-time pre-keys) to the server. To start a chat, A fetches B's bundle, runs X3DH to derive a shared secret, then uses the Double Ratchet to derive a fresh key per message (forward secrecy and post-compromise security). Server stores only ciphertext and routing metadata.

Consequences: the server cannot do server-side search or spam scanning on content (use client-side reports, metadata signals), backups need separate encryption (user passphrase or key), and key changes trigger "security code changed" warnings.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "we encrypt with TLS" and calling it E2EE.
  • Forgetting that E2EE removes server-side features.

notes.title: What interviewers look for
notes.html:
• Connection layer thinking: persistent connections, heartbeats, tuned servers, reconnect storms.
  • Numbers: 100M concurrent connections, 700k msgs/s, storage as a mailbox vs full history.
  • Delivery semantics: persist before ack, client ids, per-chat seq, dedupe, receipt ladder.
  • Offline and push handled correctly with the mailbox as truth.
  • Group fan-out trade-offs and E2EE consequences.
  • Failure thinking: gateway crash, registry stale entry, DC outage, duplicate delivery.
  • Seniors discuss multi-region, key management, abuse prevention without reading content, and cost of media.

Common interview traps.

  • Hand-waving the connection scale.
  • Ignoring ordering within a chat.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Chat is a connection-scale problem: 100M concurrent sockets across hundreds of gateway servers with heartbeats and jittered reconnects.
  • Persist then ack; at-least-once delivery plus client ids and per-chat seq gives ordered, deduplicated, effectively once delivery.
  • Session registry maps users to gateways; the message store is a per-chat or per-user mailbox in a wide-column DB.
  • Groups: inbox fan-out for small groups, shared stream with cursors for large ones.
  • Offline: mailbox is the truth, push is only a wake-up; presence and typing are ephemeral.
  • E2EE (Signal protocol) keeps servers blind to content and shapes backups, search and multi-device design.
